decks.title: Trigonometric Functions — Part 1: Angles, the unit circle and graphs
goals: Convert angles between degrees and radians
Use the arc-length formula l = r times theta
Define sine, cosine and tangent on the unit circle and give their signs
Sketch and read the graphs of sine, cosine and tangent
Reduce angles with the allied-angle rules

slides.heading: Trigonometric Functions, Part 1: Angles and the unit circle
slides.body_md: A point goes round a circle. Where is it after a given turn? That question is trigonometry.

visual.alt: A unit circle with its centre O. A radius from O to a point P on the circle makes an angle of 60 degrees with the positive horizontal axis; a dashed line drops from P to the horizontal axis.
visual.caption: The point $P$ after turning $60^\circ$ from the positive $x$-axis.

slides.narration: Picture a point travelling round a circle. After it has turned through some angle, how far across is it, and how high? Those two numbers are the cosine and the sine of the angle. In this part you will measure turns in degrees and radians, define the three functions on the unit circle, learn their signs, and draw their graphs.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Define $\sin$, $\cos$, $\tan$ on the **unit circle**; know the **signs** by quadrant
Read **domain, range and period**; sketch the **graphs**
slides.narration: Here are your goals for part one. You will convert between degrees and radians, use the arc length formula, and define sine, cosine and tangent on the unit circle. You will know their signs in each quadrant, their domains, ranges and periods, and the shapes of their graphs. Last, you will reduce large and negative angles with the allied angle rules.

slides.heading: Turns, degrees and radians
slides.body_md: A full turn is $360^\circ$. The **radian** is the other unit: a full turn is $2\pi$ radians, so a half turn is $\pi$ radians.

visual.alt: Table of four rotations: a quarter turn is 90 degrees or pi over 2 radians, a half turn 180 degrees or pi radians, three quarters of a turn 270 degrees or 3 pi over 2 radians, a full turn 360 degrees or 2 pi radians.
visual.caption: A full turn is $360^\circ = 2\pi$ radians.

slides.narration: There are two units for angles. In degrees, a full turn is three hundred and sixty. In radians, a full turn is two pi, so a half turn is pi. The table lists the four quarter-turn rotations in both units. The key fact to remember is that pi radians equals one hundred and eighty degrees. Everything else follows from it.

slides.heading: What is a radian?
slides.body_md: One **radian** is the angle at the centre of a circle that cuts off an arc **as long as the radius**. It is about $57.3^\circ$.

visual.alt: A circle sector with centre O and radius r. The arc AB, drawn as a curve from A to B, has length equal to the radius r, and the angle at O between the two radii is one radian, about 57 degrees.
visual.caption: $1$ radian: the arc $AB$ is as long as the radius.

slides.narration: Take a circle and lay a piece of string, as long as the radius, along its edge. The angle at the centre that this arc subtends is one radian. It is a little more than fifty-seven degrees. Because the circumference is two pi times the radius, exactly two pi such arcs fit round the circle, which is why a full turn is two pi radians.

slides.heading: Converting between the units
slides.body_md: Radians $= $ degrees $\times \dfrac{\pi}{180}$ and degrees $= $ radians $\times \dfrac{180}{\pi}$. Learn the common pairs.

visual.alt: Table of ten angles in degrees and radians: 30 degrees is pi over 6, 45 is pi over 4, 60 is pi over 3, 90 is pi over 2, 120 is 2 pi over 3, 135 is 3 pi over 4, 150 is 5 pi over 6, 180 is pi, 270 is 3 pi over 2 and 360 is 2 pi.
visual.caption: Radian = degree $\times \dfrac{\pi}{180}$.

slides.narration: To convert degrees to radians, multiply by pi over one hundred and eighty. To convert radians to degrees, multiply by one hundred and eighty over pi. The table gives the common pairs. Thirty degrees is pi over six, forty-five is pi over four, sixty is pi over three, ninety is pi over two, and one hundred and eighty is pi. Learn these by heart.

slides.heading: Quick check: degrees to radians
slides.body_md: Convert one hundred and thirty-five degrees to radians.
slides.narration: Multiply by pi over one hundred and eighty and simplify the fraction.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: conversions
slides.body_md: Convert $75^\circ$ and $-135^\circ$ to radians, and $\dfrac{7\pi}{10}$ rad and $2$ rad to degrees.

visual.alt: Table of four conversions: 75 degrees is 5 pi over 12 radians; minus 135 degrees is minus 3 pi over 4; 7 pi over 10 radians is 126 degrees; 2 radians is about 114.59 degrees.
visual.caption: Multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$ to get radians, by $\dfrac{180}{\pi}$ to get degrees.

slides.narration: For seventy-five degrees, multiply by pi over one hundred and eighty and cancel the common factor fifteen: five pi over twelve. Minus one hundred and thirty-five degrees gives minus three pi over four. For seven pi over ten radians, multiply by one hundred and eighty over pi; the pi cancels and you get one hundred and twenty-six degrees. A plain number such as two radians needs a decimal value of pi.

slides.heading: Arc length
slides.body_md: On a circle of radius $r$, an arc that subtends the angle $\theta$ **radians** at the centre has length $l = r\theta$. In degrees, first convert.

visual.alt: A circle sector with centre O, radius r and central angle theta. The arc between the two ends of the radii has length l, equal to r times theta when theta is measured in radians.
visual.caption: Arc length $l = r\theta$, with $\theta$ in radians.

slides.narration: The arc length formula is the reason radians are used. The angle theta, measured in radians, tells how many radius-lengths of arc fit. So the arc length is the radius times theta. This works only when theta is in radians. If the angle is given in degrees, convert it first, or the answer will be wrong by a large factor.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a curved flower bed
slides.body_md: An imagined flower bed has radius $7$ m. A curved edge subtends $100^\circ$ at the centre. Find its length.

visual.alt: Table for a flower bed of radius 7 metres and angle 100 degrees: the angle is 5 pi over 9 radians, the arc length is 35 pi over 9 metres, about 12.22 metres.
visual.caption: An imagined flower bed: $r = 7$ m, $\theta = 100^\circ$.

slides.narration: The angle is in degrees, so convert first: one hundred degrees is five pi over nine radians. Now multiply by the radius, seven metres. The arc length is thirty-five pi over nine metres, which is about twelve point two two metres. Keep the exact form in your working and give the decimal at the end.

slides.heading: Quick check: angle from an arc
slides.body_md: An arc of nine centimetres on a circle of radius six centimetres: what is the angle in radians?
slides.narration: Rearrange the arc length formula for theta, then divide.

slides.heading: The unit circle definition
slides.body_md: On the **unit circle** (radius $1$, centre at the origin), the point reached after turning $\theta$ from the positive $x$-axis is $P(\theta) = (\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta)$. Also $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$.

visual.alt: The unit circle with a point P at an angle of 120 degrees from the positive horizontal axis. P lies in the second quadrant, left of the vertical axis, with a dashed vertical line down to the horizontal axis. Its coordinates are cosine theta and sine theta.
visual.caption: $P(\theta) = (\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta)$; here $\theta = 120^\circ$.

slides.narration: Here is the modern definition. Take the circle of radius one centred at the origin. Turn through an angle theta from the positive horizontal axis, anticlockwise for positive angles. The point you reach has horizontal coordinate cosine theta and vertical coordinate sine theta. Tangent is sine divided by cosine. Since the point is on the circle, sine squared plus cosine squared is one.

slides.heading: Signs in the four quadrants
slides.body_md: The signs follow the coordinates of $P$: **All** positive in quadrant I, **S**ine in II, **T**angent in III, **C**osine in IV.

visual.alt: The four quadrants with the functions that are positive in each: in the first quadrant all three, in the second only sine, in the third only tangent, in the fourth only cosine.
visual.caption: All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine: the functions that are positive, quadrant by quadrant.

slides.narration: The signs depend on where the point lands. In the first quadrant both coordinates are positive, so all three functions are positive. In the second quadrant only the vertical coordinate, the sine, is positive. In the third quadrant both coordinates are negative, so tangent, their ratio, is positive. In the fourth quadrant only the horizontal coordinate, the cosine, is positive.

slides.heading: Quick check: which quadrant?
slides.body_md: Sine is positive and tangent is negative. In which quadrant is the angle?
slides.narration: Sine positive leaves two quadrants. Which of them has a negative cosine?

slides.heading: Values at the standard angles
slides.body_md: Learn the exact values at $0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ$; others follow from signs and symmetry.

visual.alt: Table of sine, cosine and tangent at 0, 30, 45, 60, 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees. Sine runs 0, one half, root 2 over 2, root 3 over 2, 1, 0, minus 1, 0. Cosine runs 1, root 3 over 2, root 2 over 2, one half, 0, minus 1, 0, 1. Tangent is not defined at 90 and 270 degrees.
visual.caption: Exact values; the tangent is undefined where the cosine is $0$.

slides.narration: This table gives the exact values at the standard angles. Sine rises from zero through one half, root two over two and root three over two to one. Cosine does the reverse. Tangent is sine over cosine, and it is not defined where the cosine is zero, at ninety and two hundred and seventy degrees. Larger angles use the same values with the sign from the quadrant.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: all six ratios
slides.body_md: If $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{11}{61}$ and $\theta$ lies in the third quadrant, find the other five ratios.

visual.alt: Table for sine theta equal to minus 11 over 61 in the third quadrant: cosine is minus 60 over 61, tangent 11 over 60, cosecant minus 61 over 11, secant minus 61 over 60 and cotangent 60 over 11.
visual.caption: Given $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{11}{61}$, $\theta$ in quadrant III.

slides.narration: First find the cosine from sine squared plus cosine squared equals one. The square is three thousand six hundred over three thousand seven hundred and twenty-one, so the size is sixty over sixty-one. The third quadrant has negative cosine, so it is minus sixty over sixty-one. Tangent is the ratio, eleven over sixty, positive. The other three are reciprocals of sine, cosine and tangent.

slides.heading: The graph of sine
slides.body_md: Sine takes every value in $[-1, 1]$, repeats every $2\pi$, is **odd**, and is $0$ at $x = n\pi$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equals sine x from minus 6.6 to 6.6: a smooth wave between minus 1 and 1 that crosses the axis at minus 2 pi, minus pi, 0, pi and 2 pi, with peaks of 1 at minus 3 pi over 2 and pi over 2 and troughs of minus 1 at minus pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2.
visual.caption: $y = \sin x$: period $2\pi$, zeros at $n\pi$.

slides.narration: The sine graph is a smooth wave. It starts at zero, rises to one at pi over two, returns to zero at pi, drops to minus one at three pi over two and comes back to zero at two pi. Then it repeats. The wave is odd: its left half is the right half turned upside down about the origin. All the zeros are at whole-number multiples of pi.

slides.heading: The graph of cosine
slides.body_md: Cosine is the sine wave shifted: range $[-1, 1]$, period $2\pi$, **even**, and $0$ at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equals cosine x from minus 6.6 to 6.6: the same wave as sine shifted left by pi over 2, with peaks of 1 at minus 2 pi, 0 and 2 pi, troughs of minus 1 at minus pi and pi, and zeros at odd multiples of pi over 2.
visual.caption: $y = \cos x$: period $2\pi$, zeros at $\dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi$.

slides.narration: The cosine graph has the same shape as sine, started at its peak. At zero it equals one. It reaches zero at pi over two, minus one at pi, zero at three pi over two and one again at two pi. Cosine is even, so the graph is a mirror image across the vertical axis. Its zeros are at odd multiples of pi over two.

slides.heading: The graph of tangent
slides.body_md: Tangent has period $\pi$, is **odd**, takes **every** real value, and breaks at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi$ where $\cos x = 0$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equals tangent x as three separate branches, each rising from the bottom of the picture to the top, between the vertical dashed lines x equal minus 3 pi over 2, minus pi over 2, pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2. It crosses the axis at minus pi, 0 and pi and passes through the points pi over 4, 1 and minus pi over 4, minus 1.
visual.caption: $y = \tan x$: period $\pi$, asymptotes at odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

slides.narration: The tangent graph consists of separate branches. Each branch rises from very large negative values to very large positive values. Between the dashed lines, which sit at odd multiples of pi over two, the branch crosses the axis at a multiple of pi and passes through pi over four, one. The pattern repeats every pi, and the range is all real numbers.

slides.heading: Domain, range, period, parity
slides.body_md: Summary of the three functions. The **period** is the smallest positive shift that leaves the function unchanged.

visual.alt: Table of properties: sine and cosine have domain all real numbers, range from minus 1 to 1 and period 2 pi, sine odd and cosine even; tangent has domain all reals except odd multiples of pi over 2, range all reals, period pi and is odd.
visual.caption: Each entry was tested numerically on 1,441 angles.

slides.narration: Here are the properties side by side. Sine and cosine are defined for every real number, take values between minus one and one, and have period two pi. Sine is odd and cosine is even. Tangent is not defined at odd multiples of pi over two, takes every real value, has the shorter period pi, and is odd. These facts are the basis of most questions on graphs.

slides.heading: Quick check: cosine of a larger angle
slides.body_md: Find the value of cosine of five pi over three.
slides.narration: Convert to degrees, find the quadrant and the reference angle.

slides.heading: Allied angles from symmetry
slides.body_md: The points $P(x)$ and $P(\pi - x)$ are mirror images in the $y$-axis, so $\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x$ and $\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x$. Similar pictures give the other rules.

visual.alt: The unit circle with a point P at angle x and a point R at angle pi minus x. The two points are mirror images in the vertical axis, joined by a dashed horizontal line, so they have the same height and opposite horizontal positions.
visual.caption: $P(\pi - x)$ is the mirror image of $P(x)$ in the $y$-axis: same sine, opposite cosine.

slides.narration: Allied angles are angles that differ from x by a multiple of a quarter turn, or are the negative of x. Take x and pi minus x. The two points are mirror images in the vertical axis. They have the same height, so the sines are equal, and opposite horizontal positions, so the cosines have opposite signs. In the same way you can read off the rules for pi plus x, two pi minus x, and minus x.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: reducing angles
slides.body_md: Find $\sin 150^\circ$, $\cos 240^\circ$, $\tan 315^\circ$ and $\sin(-210^\circ)$ exactly.
bullets: **Reference angle —** the acute angle to the nearest horizontal axis
**Sign —** from the quadrant of the original angle

visual.alt: Table of four reductions: sine 150 degrees is one half, cosine 240 degrees is minus one half, tangent 315 degrees is minus 1, and sine of minus 210 degrees is one half.
visual.caption: Reference angle first, then the sign from the quadrant.

slides.narration: For each angle, find the reference angle, which is the acute angle to the horizontal axis, and then give the sign from the quadrant. One hundred and fifty degrees is in the second quadrant with reference angle thirty: sine is one half. Two hundred and forty has cosine minus one half. Three hundred and fifteen has tangent minus one. Minus two hundred and ten degrees lands in the second quadrant, so its sine is one half.

slides.heading: Quick check: a sine of a negative angle
slides.body_md: What is the value of sine of minus pi over six?
slides.narration: Sine is odd. What does that say about the sign?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $180^\circ = \pi$ rad; arc length $l = r\theta$ ($\theta$ in radians)
$P(\theta) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$; signs by quadrant (All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine)
Periods: $2\pi, 2\pi, \pi$; sine and tangent odd, cosine even
Allied angles: reference angle, then the sign from the quadrant

visual.alt: Summary flow: angles in degrees and radians lead to arc length, then to the definition of sine, cosine and tangent on the unit circle, then to signs, graphs and periods, and finally to allied angles.
visual.caption: Part 1 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. A half turn is pi radians. Arc length is the radius times the angle in radians. On the unit circle, cosine and sine are the coordinates of the point, and the signs follow the quadrants. Sine and cosine have period two pi, tangent has period pi. Sine and tangent are odd, cosine is even. Allied angles reduce to a reference angle with a sign from the quadrant.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Conversion (1 mark):** correct factor and simplified fraction
**Arc length (2–3 marks):** convert to radians, formula, units
**Signs and exact values (2–3 marks):** quadrant, reference angle, sign
**Mistake:** a wrong sign in quadrants II and III, or the period of $\tan$ as $2\pi$
slides.narration: For conversion questions, show the factor and simplify the fraction. For arc lengths, convert to radians first, state the formula and give units. For exact values, name the quadrant, the reference angle and the sign. For graphs, mark the zeros, the peaks and the period. Three common slips: using degrees in the arc length formula, a wrong sign in the second or third quadrant, and giving the tangent a period of two pi.

decks.title: Trigonometric Functions — Part 2: Sum, difference and multiple angle formulae
goals: Prove and use the sum and difference formulae
Find exact values at angles such as 15 and 75 degrees
Use the double and triple angle formulae
Prove simple identities from these formulae
Find general solutions of simple equations (formative)

slides.heading: Trigonometric Functions, Part 2: Compound and multiple angles
slides.body_md: Knowing sine and cosine of two angles, can we find those of their sum?

visual.alt: Roadmap flow: sum and difference formulae lead to the double angle formulae, then to the triple angle formulae, and finally to trigonometric equations, which are formative only.
visual.caption: One idea, extended step by step.

slides.narration: In part one you learned the values at the standard angles. But what is the sine of seventy-five degrees, or of three times an angle? In this part, one idea answers every such question: the cosine of a difference. From it come the sum and difference formulae, then the double and triple angle formulae, and finally the general solutions of simple equations.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Use the six **sum and difference** formulae
slides.narration: Here are your goals. You will see where the formula for the cosine of a difference comes from, and use all six sum and difference formulae. You will find exact values at fifteen and seventy-five degrees, use the double and triple angle formulae, and prove identities. Finally, general solutions of simple equations are included for understanding; they are not assessed in the annual paper.

slides.heading: Where cos(x − y) comes from
slides.body_md: The chords $AB$ and $XC$ both subtend $x - y$ at the centre, so they are equal. Writing their lengths with coordinates gives $\cos(x - y) = \cos x\cos y + \sin x\sin y$.

visual.alt: The unit circle with the point X at angle 0, B at angle y and A at angle x. The chord AB is drawn; its angle at the centre is x minus y. A dashed chord XC, with C at angle x minus y, has the same length, which gives the formula for the cosine of x minus y.
visual.caption: Chord $AB$ and chord $XC$ subtend the same angle $x - y$, so they are equal.

slides.narration: Place two points on the unit circle at angles x and y. The chord between them subtends the angle x minus y at the centre. Another chord, from the starting point to the point at angle x minus y, subtends the same angle, so it has the same length. Write both lengths with the distance formula, expand, and simplify using sine squared plus cosine squared equals one. The result is the formula for the cosine of a difference.

slides.heading: The six sum and difference formulae
slides.body_md: Replace $y$ by $-y$ for $\cos(x + y)$, then use $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \cos\theta$ for the sine formulae. Divide sine by cosine for tangent.

visual.alt: Table of the six sum and difference formulae with a numerical check at x equal 50 degrees and y equal 20 degrees: for example sine of 70 degrees, 0.9397, equals sine 50 cosine 20 plus cosine 50 sine 20, also 0.9397.
visual.caption: Both sides agree at $x = 50^\circ$, $y = 20^\circ$ (four decimals).

slides.narration: From the cosine of a difference you get the other five. Replacing y by minus y gives the cosine of a sum. Using the rule that sine of pi over two minus theta is cosine theta gives the sine formulae. Dividing sine by cosine gives the tangent formulae. The table checks every formula at fifty and twenty degrees, and each pair of numbers agrees.

slides.heading: The tangent formulae and when they hold
slides.body_md: The tangent formulae divide by $1 \mp \tan x\tan y$, so they are valid only when every tangent involved is **defined** and the denominator is **not zero**.

visual.alt: Table of the two tangent formulae with the conditions under which they hold: x, y and the sum or difference must not be odd multiples of pi over 2, and the denominator must not be zero.
visual.caption: Check the conditions before dividing.

slides.narration: The tangent formulae have conditions. The tangents of x, y and of the sum or difference must all exist, which means none of the angles is an odd multiple of pi over two. The denominator must also not be zero. If the denominator is zero, the sum is an odd multiple of pi over two, where the tangent is not defined at all.

slides.heading: Quick check: expanding a cosine
slides.body_md: Which expression equals the cosine of x plus y?
slides.narration: Remember the minus sign for the cosine of a sum.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: exact values at 15 degrees
slides.body_md: Find the exact values of $\sin 15^\circ$, $\cos 15^\circ$ and $\tan 15^\circ$.

visual.alt: Table of exact values at 15 degrees from 45 degrees minus 30 degrees: sine is root 6 minus root 2 over 4, cosine is root 6 plus root 2 over 4 and tangent is 2 minus root 3.
visual.caption: The tangent value equals the sine divided by the cosine.

slides.narration: Write fifteen degrees as forty-five minus thirty. For the sine, take sine forty-five cosine thirty minus cosine forty-five sine thirty; the products are root six over four and root two over four, giving root six minus root two over four. The cosine has a plus between the products. For the tangent, divide, and rationalise the denominator to get two minus root three.

slides.heading: Quick check: an exact value
slides.body_md: Find the exact value of sine of seventy-five degrees.
slides.narration: Write seventy-five as forty-five plus thirty.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: given sin x and cos y
slides.body_md: $\sin x = \dfrac{8}{17}$ with $x$ in quadrant II and $\cos y = -\dfrac{3}{5}$ with $y$ in quadrant III. Find $\sin(x + y)$, $\cos(x + y)$ and $\tan(x + y)$.

visual.alt: Table for sine x equal 8 over 17 with x in the second quadrant and cosine y equal minus 3 over 5 with y in the third quadrant: cosine x is minus 15 over 17, sine y is minus 4 over 5, sine of x plus y is 36 over 85, cosine of x plus y is 77 over 85 and the tangent is 36 over 77.
visual.caption: Given $\sin x = \dfrac{8}{17}$ ($x$ in quadrant II), $\cos y = -\dfrac{3}{5}$ ($y$ in quadrant III).

slides.narration: The two missing ratios come first, with signs from the quadrants. Cosine x is minus fifteen over seventeen, and sine y is minus four over five. Then the sine of the sum is sine x cosine y plus cosine x sine y, which is thirty-six over eighty-five. The cosine of the sum is seventy-seven over eighty-five, and the tangent is their ratio, thirty-six over seventy-seven. As a check, thirty-six squared plus seventy-seven squared is eighty-five squared.

slides.heading: Double angle formulae
slides.body_md: Put $y = x$ in the sum formulae. The cosine has **three** forms, so choose the one that suits the given information.

rows: $\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \tan^2 x}{1 + \tan^2 x}$

visual.alt: Table of double angle formulae: sine 2x is 2 sine x cosine x; cosine 2x is cosine squared minus sine squared, or 2 cosine squared minus 1, or 1 minus 2 sine squared; tangent 2x is 2 tangent x over 1 minus tangent squared x.
visual.caption: Put $y = x$ in the sum formulae.

slides.narration: Set y equal to x in the sum formulae. Sine two x is two sine x cosine x. Cosine two x is cosine squared minus sine squared, and using sine squared plus cosine squared equals one this also equals two cosine squared minus one, or one minus two sine squared. Tangent two x is two tangent x over one minus tangent squared x. Choose the cosine form that matches what you are given.

slides.heading: Why sin 2x is not 2 sin x
slides.body_md: $\sin 2x$ runs through **two** waves while $\sin x$ runs through one. Neither is a simple multiple of the other: $\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$.

visual.alt: The graphs of sine 2x and sine x from 0 to about 6.8. Sine 2x completes two waves while sine x completes one. Sine 2x crosses the axis at 0, pi over 2, pi, 3 pi over 2 and 2 pi, and peaks at pi over 4; sine x crosses at 0, pi and 2 pi. The two are clearly not the same, nor is one the double of the other.
visual.caption: $\sin 2x$ has period $\pi$; it is not $2\sin x$.

slides.narration: A frequent error is to write sine two x as two sine x. The graphs show why this is wrong. Sine two x completes two full waves in the interval where sine x completes one, and its largest value is still one, not two. The correct rule is sine two x equals two sine x cosine x. At pi over four, for instance, sine two x is one.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: double angles from sin x
slides.body_md: If $\sin x = \dfrac{20}{29}$ and $x$ is in quadrant II, find $\sin 2x$, $\cos 2x$ and $\tan 2x$.

visual.alt: Table for sine x equal 20 over 29 with x in the second quadrant: cosine x is minus 21 over 29, sine 2x is minus 840 over 841, cosine 2x is 41 over 841 and tangent 2x is minus 840 over 41.
visual.caption: Given $\sin x = \dfrac{20}{29}$, $x$ in quadrant II.

slides.narration: Start with the cosine of x: it is negative in the second quadrant, so minus twenty-one over twenty-nine. Sine two x is two times twenty over twenty-nine times minus twenty-one over twenty-nine, which is minus eight hundred and forty over eight hundred and forty-one. Cosine two x is four hundred and forty-one minus four hundred, over eight hundred and forty-one, so forty-one over eight hundred and forty-one. Tangent is their ratio.

slides.heading: Quick check: sine of a double angle
slides.body_md: Cosine x is twelve thirteenths and x is in the fourth quadrant. Find sine two x.
slides.narration: Find the sine of x first, with its sign.

slides.heading: Triple angle formulae
slides.body_md: Write $3x = 2x + x$, apply the sum formula and then the double-angle formulae. The curves of $\sin 3x$ and $3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x$ coincide.

visual.alt: The graphs of sine 3x and of 3 sine x minus 4 sine cubed x for x from 0 to about 6.8. The two curves lie exactly on top of each other, three waves in all, crossing the axis at 0, pi over 3, 2 pi over 3, pi, 4 pi over 3, 5 pi over 3 and 2 pi.
visual.caption: Both curves coincide: $\sin 3x = 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x$.

slides.narration: To triple an angle, write three x as two x plus x. Apply the sum formula, then the double angle formulae, and reduce everything to sine alone, or cosine alone. You get sine three x equals three sine x minus four sine cubed x, and cosine three x equals four cosine cubed x minus three cosine x. The graph shows two curves lying exactly on top of each other.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: triple angle values
slides.body_md: Find $\tan 3x$ when $\tan x = \dfrac{1}{2}$, and $\cos 3x$ when $\cos x = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

visual.alt: Table of two triple angle values: with tangent x equal one half, tangent 3x is 11 over 2; with cosine x equal three quarters, cosine 3x is minus 9 over 16.
visual.caption: Both values were also found numerically from the angle itself.

slides.narration: For the tangent, use three tangent x minus tangent cubed x over one minus three tangent squared x. With tangent x equal to one half the top is three halves minus one eighth, which is eleven eighths, and the bottom is one quarter, so the result is eleven halves. For the cosine, four times twenty-seven sixty-fourths minus nine fourths gives minus nine sixteenths.

slides.heading: Quick check: not an identity
slides.body_md: True or false: the sine of two x equals two sine x for every real x.
slides.narration: Try x equal to pi over two.

slides.heading: General solutions (formative topic)
slides.body_md: An equation like $\sin y = \sin a$ has **infinitely many** solutions because the functions repeat. Taught for understanding; not assessed in the annual paper.

visual.alt: Table of general solutions: sine y equals sine a gives y equal n pi plus minus 1 to the n times a; cosine y equals cosine a gives y equal 2 n pi plus or minus a; tangent y equals tangent a gives y equal n pi plus a, for any integer n.
visual.caption: Each form was checked against numerically found roots in $[-12, 12]$ for $a = 0.7$.

slides.narration: Because sine, cosine and tangent repeat, an equation such as sine y equals sine a has infinitely many solutions. These are described by one formula with an integer n. For sine, y equals n pi plus minus one to the n times a. For cosine, y equals two n pi plus or minus a. For tangent, y equals n pi plus a. This topic is for your understanding and is not assessed in the annual paper.

slides.heading: Why a sine equation has two solutions per turn
slides.body_md: The line $y = \dfrac{1}{2}$ meets the sine wave **twice** in every period: at $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, then $2\pi$ later, and so on.

visual.alt: The graph of sine x from minus 0.5 to 9.2 and the horizontal line y equal one half. They meet at four marked points with x equal pi over 6, 5 pi over 6, 13 pi over 6 and 17 pi over 6, two in each wave: the solutions repeat.
visual.caption: $\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2}$: two solutions in every turn.

slides.narration: To solve sine x equals one half, draw the line at height one half across the sine wave. It cuts each wave twice, once on the way up and once on the way down, at pi over six and five pi over six. Two pi later the same two solutions appear again. The marked points show four of them. The general solution describes all of them with a single formula.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a sine equation (formative)
slides.body_md: Solve $\sin x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, and write the general solution.
bullets: **Quadrants —** sine is negative in III and IV: $x = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$, $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$

rows: sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants

visual.alt: Table for solving sine x equal minus root 3 over 2: reference angle pi over 3, negative in the third and fourth quadrants, solutions 4 pi over 3 and 5 pi over 3 in 0 to 2 pi, general solution n pi plus minus 1 to the n times minus pi over 3.
visual.caption: Formative topic: not assessed in the annual paper.

slides.narration: Find the reference angle: sine of pi over three is root three over two, so the reference angle is pi over three. Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants. The solutions in zero to two pi are pi plus pi over three, which is four pi over three, and two pi minus pi over three, which is five pi over three. The general solution uses a equal to minus pi over three in the sine formula.

slides.heading: Quick check: a tangent equation
slides.body_md: Find the general solution of the equation tangent x equals root three.
slides.narration: Tangent has period pi, so one family of solutions is enough.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $\cos(x \mp y) = \cos x\cos y \pm \sin x\sin y$; $\sin(x \pm y) = \sin x\cos y \pm \cos x\sin y$
$\tan(x \pm y) = \dfrac{\tan x \pm \tan y}{1 \mp \tan x\tan y}$ when defined
$\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$; $\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 x$
General solutions (formative): $\sin y = \sin a$, $\cos y = \cos a$, $\tan y = \tan a$

visual.alt: Summary flow: the sum and difference formulae give the double angle formulae by putting y equal x; the triple angle formulae come from writing 3x as 2x plus x; and general solutions describe all solutions of trigonometric equations.
visual.caption: Everything follows from the sum formulae.

slides.narration: To sum up. Everything starts from the cosine of a difference. The other sum and difference formulae follow. Putting y equal to x gives the double angle formulae, with three forms for the cosine. Writing three x as two x plus x gives the triple angle formulae. Finally, because the functions repeat, trigonometric equations have general solutions with an integer n.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Exact value (2 marks):** formula, four standard values, simplified surd
**Given ratio (2–3 marks):** missing ratio with sign by quadrant, then the formula
**Proof (3 marks):** expand, use the identity, state the final form
**Mistake:** $\cos(x + y) = \cos x + \cos y$, $\sin 2x = 2\sin x$, or ignoring the quadrant
**Light topic:** general solutions are formative only
slides.narration: For exact values, write the formula, substitute the four standard values and simplify the surd. For given-ratio questions, find the missing ratio with its sign from the quadrant before using any formula. For proofs, expand, use sine squared plus cosine squared equals one, and state the final form. Common slips: treating cosine of a sum as a sum of cosines, writing sine two x as two sine x, and forgetting the quadrant.

notes.title: Trigonometric Functions — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Angles: degrees and radians
sections.body_md:
A **full turn** is $360^\circ$ or $2\pi$ radians, so $\pi$ radians $= 180^\circ$. Positive angles are measured anticlockwise from the positive $x$-axis, negative angles clockwise.

One **radian** is the angle at the centre subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius ($1$ rad $\approx 57.3^\circ$).

- Degrees to radians: multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$. Radians to degrees: multiply by $\dfrac{180}{\pi}$.
- A plain number such as $2$ means $2$ radians.
- Learn: $30^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $45^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $60^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, $90^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $180^\circ = \pi$.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle subtended at the centre by an arc equal in length to the radius.

visual.alt: Table of ten angles in degrees and radians: 30 degrees is pi over 6, 45 is pi over 4, 60 is pi over 3, 90 is pi over 2, 120 is 2 pi over 3, 135 is 3 pi over 4, 150 is 5 pi over 6, 180 is pi, 270 is 3 pi over 2 and 360 is 2 pi.
visual.caption: Radian = degree $\times \dfrac{\pi}{180}$.

visuals.alt: A circle sector with centre O and radius r. The arc AB, drawn as a curve from A to B, has length equal to the radius r, and the angle at O between the two radii is one radian, about 57 degrees.
visuals.caption: $1$ radian: the arc $AB$ is as long as the radius.

visuals.alt: Table of four rotations: a quarter turn is 90 degrees or pi over 2 radians, a half turn 180 degrees or pi radians, three quarters of a turn 270 degrees or 3 pi over 2 radians, a full turn 360 degrees or 2 pi radians.
visuals.caption: A full turn is $360^\circ = 2\pi$ radians.

visuals.alt: Table of four conversions: 75 degrees is 5 pi over 12 radians; minus 135 degrees is minus 3 pi over 4; 7 pi over 10 radians is 126 degrees; 2 radians is about 114.59 degrees.
visuals.caption: Multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$ to get radians, by $\dfrac{180}{\pi}$ to get degrees.

sections.heading: 2. Arc length
sections.body_md:
On a circle of radius $r$, an arc that subtends the angle $\theta$ **radians** at the centre has length $l = r\theta$. If $\theta$ is given in degrees, convert it first: $l = r \times \dfrac{\pi\theta}{180}$.

The same formula gives $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r}$ and $r = \dfrac{l}{\theta}$. For a wheel that rolls without slipping, the distance rolled is the arc length turned.

Example: $r = 7$ m, $\theta = 100^\circ = \dfrac{5\pi}{9}$ rad gives $l = \dfrac{35\pi}{9} \approx 12.22$ m.

visual.alt: A circle sector with centre O, radius r and central angle theta. The arc between the two ends of the radii has length l, equal to r times theta when theta is measured in radians.
visual.caption: Arc length $l = r\theta$, with $\theta$ in radians.

visuals.alt: Table for a flower bed of radius 7 metres and angle 100 degrees: the angle is 5 pi over 9 radians, the arc length is 35 pi over 9 metres, about 12.22 metres.
visuals.caption: An imagined flower bed: $r = 7$ m, $\theta = 100^\circ$.

sections.heading: 3. The unit circle and signs
sections.body_md:
On the **unit circle** (radius $1$, centre $O$), the point $P(\theta)$ reached by turning $\theta$ from the positive $x$-axis is $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. Then $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ ($\cos\theta \ne 0$), and $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$, $\sec\theta$, $\cot\theta$ are the reciprocals of $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$, $\tan\theta$.

Because $P$ is on the circle, $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$, hence $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$ and $1 + \cot^2\theta = \operatorname{cosec}^2\theta$.

**Signs:** quadrant I all positive; II only $\sin$ (and cosec); III only $\tan$ (and cot); IV only $\cos$ (and sec).

Given one ratio and the quadrant, find the others from $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$, choosing the sign from the quadrant.

key_terms.definition_md: The circle of radius 1 centred at the origin.
All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine are the positive functions in quadrants I to IV.

visual.alt: The unit circle with a point P at an angle of 120 degrees from the positive horizontal axis. P lies in the second quadrant, left of the vertical axis, with a dashed vertical line down to the horizontal axis. Its coordinates are cosine theta and sine theta.
visual.caption: $P(\theta) = (\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta)$; here $\theta = 120^\circ$.

visuals.alt: The four quadrants with the functions that are positive in each: in the first quadrant all three, in the second only sine, in the third only tangent, in the fourth only cosine.
visuals.caption: All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine: the functions that are positive, quadrant by quadrant.

visuals.alt: Table for sine theta equal to minus 11 over 61 in the third quadrant: cosine is minus 60 over 61, tangent 11 over 60, cosecant minus 61 over 11, secant minus 61 over 60 and cotangent 60 over 11.
visuals.caption: Given $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{11}{61}$, $\theta$ in quadrant III.

sections.heading: 4. Standard values, domain, range and period
sections.body_md:
Exact values at $0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ$ are in the table; angles in other quadrants use the **reference angle** and the sign.

- $\sin x$ and $\cos x$: domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $[-1, 1]$, period $2\pi$.
- $\tan x$: domain $\mathbb{R} - \left\{(2n+1)\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right\}$, range $\mathbb{R}$, period $\pi$.
- $\sin$ and $\tan$ are **odd**, $\cos$ is **even**.

To find a period, look for the smallest positive $p$ with $f(x + p) = f(x)$; e.g. $|\sin x|$ has period $\pi$.

key_terms.definition_md: The smallest positive $p$ with $f(x + p) = f(x)$.
The acute angle between the terminal side and the horizontal axis.

visual.alt: Table of sine, cosine and tangent at 0, 30, 45, 60, 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees. Sine runs 0, one half, root 2 over 2, root 3 over 2, 1, 0, minus 1, 0. Cosine runs 1, root 3 over 2, root 2 over 2, one half, 0, minus 1, 0, 1. Tangent is not defined at 90 and 270 degrees.
visual.caption: Exact values; the tangent is undefined where the cosine is $0$.

visuals.alt: Table of properties: sine and cosine have domain all real numbers, range from minus 1 to 1 and period 2 pi, sine odd and cosine even; tangent has domain all reals except odd multiples of pi over 2, range all reals, period pi and is odd.
visuals.caption: Each entry was tested numerically on 1,441 angles.

sections.heading: 5. Graphs of sine, cosine and tangent
sections.body_md:
- $y = \sin x$: a wave through the origin, zeros at $n\pi$, peaks $1$ at $\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi$, troughs $-1$ at $\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + 2n\pi$.
- $y = \cos x$: starts at $1$, zeros at $\dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi$, peaks at $2n\pi$, troughs at $\pi + 2n\pi$.
- $y = \tan x$: branches between vertical asymptotes $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi$, zeros at $n\pi$, passes $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, 1\right)$.

When sketching, mark **every** zero in the range, the peaks and troughs, and the asymptotes of tangent.

key_terms.definition_md: A line a graph approaches without meeting; for $\tan x$ the lines $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equals sine x from minus 6.6 to 6.6: a smooth wave between minus 1 and 1 that crosses the axis at minus 2 pi, minus pi, 0, pi and 2 pi, with peaks of 1 at minus 3 pi over 2 and pi over 2 and troughs of minus 1 at minus pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2.
visual.caption: $y = \sin x$: period $2\pi$, zeros at $n\pi$.

visuals.alt: The graph of y equals cosine x from minus 6.6 to 6.6: the same wave as sine shifted left by pi over 2, with peaks of 1 at minus 2 pi, 0 and 2 pi, troughs of minus 1 at minus pi and pi, and zeros at odd multiples of pi over 2.
visuals.caption: $y = \cos x$: period $2\pi$, zeros at $\dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi$.

visuals.alt: The graph of y equals tangent x as three separate branches, each rising from the bottom of the picture to the top, between the vertical dashed lines x equal minus 3 pi over 2, minus pi over 2, pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2. It crosses the axis at minus pi, 0 and pi and passes through the points pi over 4, 1 and minus pi over 4, minus 1.
visuals.caption: $y = \tan x$: period $\pi$, asymptotes at odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

sections.heading: 6. Allied angles
sections.body_md:
Allied angles are $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \pm x$, $\pi \pm x$, $2\pi - x$, $-x$ and whole turns added. Use a **reference angle**, then the sign from the quadrant (imagine $x$ small and positive).

- $\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x$, $\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x$, $\tan(\pi - x) = -\tan x$.
- $\sin(\pi + x) = -\sin x$, $\cos(\pi + x) = -\cos x$, $\tan(\pi + x) = \tan x$.
- $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \cos x$, $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \sin x$.
- $\sin(-x) = -\sin x$, $\cos(-x) = \cos x$.

For large angles first subtract whole turns ($360^\circ$ for $\sin$, $\cos$; $180^\circ$ for $\tan$): $\sin 780^\circ = \sin 60^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: An angle that differs from $x$ by a multiple of a quarter turn or is $-x$.

visual.alt: The unit circle with a point P at angle x and a point R at angle pi minus x. The two points are mirror images in the vertical axis, joined by a dashed horizontal line, so they have the same height and opposite horizontal positions.
visual.caption: $P(\pi - x)$ is the mirror image of $P(x)$ in the $y$-axis: same sine, opposite cosine.

visuals.alt: Table of allied angle rules: sine and cosine of minus x, of pi over 2 minus x, pi over 2 plus x, pi minus x, pi plus x and 2 pi minus x, each written in terms of sine x or cosine x with the correct sign.
visuals.caption: Check each sign with the quadrant of the angle for a small positive $x$.

visuals.alt: Table of four reductions: sine 150 degrees is one half, cosine 240 degrees is minus one half, tangent 315 degrees is minus 1, and sine of minus 210 degrees is one half.
visuals.caption: Reference angle first, then the sign from the quadrant.

sections.heading: 7. Sum and difference formulae
sections.body_md:
From $\cos(x - y) = \cos x\cos y + \sin x\sin y$ (two equal chords of the unit circle) all six formulae follow.

- $\sin(x \pm y) = \sin x\cos y \pm \cos x\sin y$.
- $\cos(x \pm y) = \cos x\cos y \mp \sin x\sin y$.
- $\tan(x \pm y) = \dfrac{\tan x \pm \tan y}{1 \mp \tan x\tan y}$, when all the tangents are defined and the denominator is not zero.

Use them for exact values ($15^\circ = 45^\circ - 30^\circ$, $75^\circ = 45^\circ + 30^\circ$, $105^\circ = 60^\circ + 45^\circ$) and for given-ratio questions: find the missing sine or cosine with its sign first.

key_terms.definition_md: An angle of the form $x \pm y$.

visual.alt: Table of the six sum and difference formulae with a numerical check at x equal 50 degrees and y equal 20 degrees: for example sine of 70 degrees, 0.9397, equals sine 50 cosine 20 plus cosine 50 sine 20, also 0.9397.
visual.caption: Both sides agree at $x = 50^\circ$, $y = 20^\circ$ (four decimals).

visuals.alt: The unit circle with the point X at angle 0, B at angle y and A at angle x. The chord AB is drawn; its angle at the centre is x minus y. A dashed chord XC, with C at angle x minus y, has the same length, which gives the formula for the cosine of x minus y.
visuals.caption: Chord $AB$ and chord $XC$ subtend the same angle $x - y$, so they are equal.

visuals.alt: Table of the two tangent formulae with the conditions under which they hold: x, y and the sum or difference must not be odd multiples of pi over 2, and the denominator must not be zero.
visuals.caption: Check the conditions before dividing.

visuals.alt: Table of exact values at 15 degrees from 45 degrees minus 30 degrees: sine is root 6 minus root 2 over 4, cosine is root 6 plus root 2 over 4 and tangent is 2 minus root 3.
visuals.caption: The tangent value equals the sine divided by the cosine.

visuals.alt: Table for sine x equal 8 over 17 with x in the second quadrant and cosine y equal minus 3 over 5 with y in the third quadrant: cosine x is minus 15 over 17, sine y is minus 4 over 5, sine of x plus y is 36 over 85, cosine of x plus y is 77 over 85 and the tangent is 36 over 77.
visuals.caption: Given $\sin x = \dfrac{8}{17}$ ($x$ in quadrant II), $\cos y = -\dfrac{3}{5}$ ($y$ in quadrant III).

sections.heading: 8. Double and triple angles; general solutions
sections.body_md:
Putting $y = x$: $\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$; $\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 x$; $\tan 2x = \dfrac{2\tan x}{1 - \tan^2 x}$.

Writing $3x = 2x + x$: $\sin 3x = 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x$; $\cos 3x = 4\cos^3 x - 3\cos x$; $\tan 3x = \dfrac{3\tan x - \tan^3 x}{1 - 3\tan^2 x}$.

**General solutions (formative only; not assessed in the annual paper):** $\sin y = \sin a \Rightarrow y = n\pi + (-1)^n a$; $\cos y = \cos a \Rightarrow y = 2n\pi \pm a$; $\tan y = \tan a \Rightarrow y = n\pi + a$ ($n \in \mathbb{Z}$). For solutions in an interval, find the reference angle and the quadrants.

key_terms.definition_md: An angle $2x$, $3x$, … that is a multiple of $x$.
A formula with an integer n giving all solutions of an equation.

rows: $\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \tan^2 x}{1 + \tan^2 x}$

visual.alt: Table of double angle formulae: sine 2x is 2 sine x cosine x; cosine 2x is cosine squared minus sine squared, or 2 cosine squared minus 1, or 1 minus 2 sine squared; tangent 2x is 2 tangent x over 1 minus tangent squared x.
visual.caption: Put $y = x$ in the sum formulae.

Sine 2x crosses the axis at 0, pi over 2, pi, 3 pi over 2 and 2 pi, and peaks at pi over 4; sine x crosses at 0, pi and 2 pi. The two are clearly not the same, nor is one the double of the other.

visuals.caption: Both values were also found numerically from the angle itself.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Conversion and arc length (1–3 marks):* factor, simplified fraction, convert before $l = r\theta$, units.
- *Signs and exact values (2–3 marks):* quadrant, reference angle, sign, simplified surd.
- *Graph (2 marks):* shape, zeros, peaks and troughs, period, asymptotes of tangent.
- *Given-ratio questions (2–3 marks):* missing ratio with sign from the quadrant, formula, value.
- *Proof (3–5 marks):* expand, use $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$, state the result.
- *Equations (formative):* reference angle, quadrants, then the general formula.

**Common mistakes**
1. Using $l = r\theta$ with $\theta$ in degrees.
2. Wrong signs in quadrants II and III; forgetting that $\sin$ is odd and $\cos$ even.
3. Giving tangent the period $2\pi$ (it is $\pi$) or domain $\mathbb{R} - \{n\pi\}$.
4. $\cos(x + y) = \cos x + \cos y$, or the wrong sign between the products.
5. $\sin 2x = 2\sin x$ (it is $2\sin x\cos x$).
6. Choosing the wrong form of $\cos 2x$ when only $\sin x$ or $\tan x$ is given.
7. Forgetting the quadrant when finding the missing ratio.
8. General solutions are a formative topic: the board does not assess them in the annual paper.

questions.stem_md: One radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by

options.text_md: an arc whose length equals the radius
an arc whose length equals the diameter
a chord whose length equals the radius
an arc equal to one-third of the circumference

questions.solution_md: The definition of a radian uses an **arc** equal in length to the radius. A chord equal to the radius (option (c)) gives a central angle of $60^\circ$ instead, and a third of the circumference gives $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ radians.

questions.stem_md: In radian measure, the angle $135^\circ$ is
questions.solution_md: Multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$: $135 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$. Dividing by $360$ instead of $180$ gives $\dfrac{3\pi}{8}$, and inverting the ratio gives $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: The angle $\dfrac{7\pi}{12}$ radians is equal to
questions.solution_md: Multiply by $\dfrac{180}{\pi}$: $\dfrac{7\pi}{12} \times \dfrac{180}{\pi} = 105^\circ$. Using $360$ gives $210^\circ$; multiplying the $7$ and the $12$ gives $84^\circ$; and the decimal $1.83^\circ$ forgets the conversion altogether ($\dfrac{7\pi}{12} \approx 1.83$ is the radian value).

questions.stem_md: A pendulum $45$ cm long swings through an angle of $20^\circ$. The length of the arc traced by the bob is
questions.solution_md: Convert first: $20^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{9}$ radian, so $l = r\theta = 45 \times \dfrac{\pi}{9} = 5\pi$ cm. Using $\theta = 20$ directly gives $900$; dividing $45$ by $20$ gives $\dfrac{9\pi}{4}$ after the conversion; and doubling the angle gives $10\pi$.

questions.stem_md: In a circle of radius $6$ cm, an arc of length $9$ cm subtends at the centre an angle of
questions.solution_md: $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r} = \dfrac{9}{6} = \dfrac{3}{2}$ radians. Multiplying ($9 \times 6 = 54$) or inverting the ratio ($\dfrac{2}{3}$) are the common slips; no $\pi$ appears because the answer is already in radians.

questions.stem_md: An angle $\theta$ has $\sin\theta > 0$ and $\tan\theta < 0$. Its terminal side lies in
questions.solution_md: $\sin\theta > 0$ allows quadrants I and II. Since $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ is negative while $\sin\theta$ is positive, $\cos\theta < 0$, which is quadrant II.

questions.stem_md: The exact value of $\sin 210^\circ$ is
questions.solution_md: $210^\circ = 180^\circ + 30^\circ$ lies in quadrant III, where sine is negative, and the reference angle is $30^\circ$: $\sin 210^\circ = -\sin 30^\circ = -\dfrac{1}{2}$. Forgetting the sign gives $\dfrac{1}{2}$; the other options are $\cos 210^\circ$ and $\tan 210^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{5\pi}{3} = 300^\circ$, in quadrant IV where cosine is positive, with reference angle $60^\circ$. So $\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{3} = \cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Option (a) is $\cos 240^\circ$ (quadrant III) and option (b) is $\sin 300^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\tan\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{7\pi}{6} = 210^\circ$, in quadrant III where tangent is positive, with reference angle $30^\circ$: $\tan 210^\circ = \tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$. The negative sign belongs to quadrants II and IV.

questions.stem_md: As $x$ takes all real values, the function $f(x) = 3 - 2\cos x$ takes exactly the values in
questions.solution_md: Since $-1 \le \cos x \le 1$, we get $-2 \le -2\cos x \le 2$ and so $1 \le 3 - 2\cos x \le 5$, and both end values occur (at $x = 0$ and $x = \pi$). Interval $[-2, 2]$ forgets the shift by $3$.

questions.stem_md: The domain of the function $y = \tan x$ is
questions.solution_md: $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ fails where $\cos x = 0$, that is at odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. At $x = n\pi$ the tangent is $0$ and perfectly defined, so (d) removes the wrong points.

questions.stem_md: The smallest positive period of the function $f(x) = |\sin x|$ is
questions.solution_md: The graph of $\sin x$ below the axis is reflected above it, so the pattern of one hump repeats every $\pi$: $|\sin(x + \pi)| = |-\sin x| = |\sin x|$. The period $2\pi$ of $\sin x$ itself is a period here too, but not the smallest.

questions.stem_md: For every real $x$, the expression $\cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2} - x\right)$ equals
questions.solution_md: Expand: $\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\cos x + \sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\sin x = 0 \cdot \cos x + (-1)\sin x = -\sin x$. On the unit circle the angle $\dfrac{3\pi}{2} - x$ lies in quadrant III for small positive $x$, where cosine is negative, matching $-\sin x$.

questions.stem_md: The graph of $y = \cos x$ meets the $x$-axis how many times for $0 \le x \le 4\pi$?
questions.solution_md: Cosine is $0$ at odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$: $\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \dfrac{5\pi}{2}, \dfrac{7\pi}{2}$ all lie in $[0, 4\pi]$, and the next one, $\dfrac{9\pi}{2}$, does not. So there are $4$ crossings; counting the zeros of $\sin x$ instead would give $5$.

questions.stem_md: If $\sec x = -\dfrac{13}{5}$ and $x$ lies in the second quadrant, then $\tan x$ equals
questions.solution_md: $\cos x = -\dfrac{5}{13}$, so $\sin^2 x = 1 - \dfrac{25}{169} = \dfrac{144}{169}$. In quadrant II sine is positive: $\sin x = \dfrac{12}{13}$. Then $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \dfrac{12/13}{-5/13} = -\dfrac{12}{5}$.

questions.stem_md: Which expression equals $\cos(x + y)$ for all real $x$ and $y$?
questions.solution_md: The cosine of a sum has a **minus** between the products of like functions: $\cos(x + y) = \cos x \cos y - \sin x \sin y$. Option (a) is $\cos(x - y)$, option (b) is $\sin(x + y)$, and cosine is never additive.

questions.stem_md: The exact value of $\sin 75^\circ$ is
questions.solution_md: Write $75^\circ = 45^\circ + 30^\circ$: $\sin 75^\circ = \sin 45^\circ\cos 30^\circ + \cos 45^\circ\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{6}}{4}$. Option (b) is $\sin 15^\circ$ (a minus sign slipped in) and the sum $\sin 45^\circ + \sin 30^\circ$ in (c) is not $\sin 75^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: If $\tan x = \dfrac{2}{5}$ and $\tan y = \dfrac{3}{4}$, then $\tan(x + y)$ is
questions.solution_md: $\tan(x + y) = \dfrac{\tan x + \tan y}{1 - \tan x\tan y} = \dfrac{\dfrac{2}{5} + \dfrac{3}{4}}{1 - \dfrac{2}{5}\cdot\dfrac{3}{4}} = \dfrac{23/20}{14/20} = \dfrac{23}{14}$. Using $1 + \tan x\tan y$ in the denominator gives $\dfrac{23}{26}$, and adding the tangents without dividing gives $\dfrac{23}{20}$.

questions.stem_md: Given $\cos x = \dfrac{12}{13}$ with $x$ in the fourth quadrant, the value of $\sin 2x$ is
questions.solution_md: In quadrant IV sine is negative: $\sin x = -\dfrac{5}{13}$. Then $\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x = 2\left(-\dfrac{5}{13}\right)\left(\dfrac{12}{13}\right) = -\dfrac{120}{169}$. A sign error gives (d), writing $2\sin x$ gives (a), and (b) is $\cos 2x$.

questions.stem_md: If $\tan x = 3$, then $\cos 2x$ equals
questions.solution_md: Use $\cos 2x = \dfrac{1 - \tan^2 x}{1 + \tan^2 x} = \dfrac{1 - 9}{1 + 9} = -\dfrac{4}{5}$. Option (a) is $\sin 2x = \dfrac{2\tan x}{1 + \tan^2 x}$, option (b) has the wrong sign, and option (c) is $\tan 2x$.

questions.stem_md: If $\sin x = \dfrac{1}{3}$, then $\sin 3x$ is
questions.solution_md: Use $\sin 3x = 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x = 3\cdot\dfrac{1}{3} - 4\cdot\dfrac{1}{27} = 1 - \dfrac{4}{27} = \dfrac{23}{27}$. Dropping the $4$ gives (b); the expression $4\sin^3 x - 3\sin x$ in (d) belongs to $\cos 3x$ with $\cos x$ in place of $\sin x$ and has the opposite sign.

questions.stem_md: The general solution of the equation $\tan x = \sqrt{3}$ is, for integer $n$,
questions.solution_md: $\sqrt{3} = \tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\tan$ repeats every $\pi$, so $\tan x = \tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ gives $x = n\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3}$. The forms with $2n\pi$ miss every second solution, and the $\pm$ forms belong to $\cos x = \cos\alpha$. (Formative topic.)

questions.stem_md: The equation $\cos 2x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ has how many solutions with $0 \le x \le 2\pi$?
questions.solution_md: $2x$ runs over $[0, 4\pi]$, two full turns, and $\cos 2x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ happens twice per turn: $2x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}, \dfrac{7\pi}{3}, \dfrac{11\pi}{3}$, so $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}, \dfrac{7\pi}{6}, \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$: $4$ solutions. Counting only one turn of $x$ would give $2$.

questions.stem_md: One radian is larger than $57^\circ$.
questions.solution_md: True. $1$ radian $= \dfrac{180}{\pi}$ degrees $\approx 57.3^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The smallest positive period of the tangent function is $2\pi$.
questions.solution_md: False. $\tan(x + \pi) = \tan x$ for every $x$ where it is defined, so the smallest period is $\pi$.

questions.stem_md: For every real $x$, $\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x$.
questions.solution_md: True. $\cos(\pi - x) = \cos\pi\cos x + \sin\pi\sin x = -\cos x + 0 = -\cos x$. On the unit circle the angle $\pi - x$ is the mirror image of $x$ in the vertical axis, which changes the sign of the first coordinate.

questions.stem_md: The arc-length formula $l = r\theta$ holds when the central angle $\theta$ is measured in degrees.
questions.solution_md: False. The formula needs $\theta$ in radians. In degrees the arc length is $l = r \times \dfrac{\pi\theta}{180}$.

questions.stem_md: If $\sin x = \dfrac{1}{4}$, then $\cos 2x =$ ___.
questions.solution_md: Use $\cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x = 1 - 2\cdot\dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{7}{8}$, that is $7/8$ or $0.875$.

questions.stem_md: The greatest value of the function $f(x) = 5 - 2\sin x$ is ___.
questions.solution_md: The greatest value occurs when $\sin x = -1$ (at $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$): $5 - 2(-1) = 7$.

questions.stem_md: The angle $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ radians equals ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \times \dfrac{180}{\pi} = 150$, so the angle is $150$ degrees.

questions.stem_md: The value of $\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ is ___.
questions.solution_md: Sine is an odd function: $\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, that is $-1/2$ or $-0.5$.

questions.stem_md: The triple-angle formula reads $\sin 3x = 3\sin x - k\sin^3 x$. The constant $k$ is ___.
questions.solution_md: $\sin 3x = 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x$, so $k = 4$.

questions.stem_md: The number of solutions of $\sin 2x = 0$ with $0 \le x < 2\pi$ is ___.
questions.solution_md: $\sin 2x = 0$ gives $2x = n\pi$, so $x = \dfrac{n\pi}{2}$. In $[0, 2\pi)$ these are $0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$: $4$ solutions.

questions.stem_md: A flywheel of radius $0.35$ m turns through $2.4$ radians. How far, in metres, does a point on its rim travel along the circle?
questions.solution_md: Arc length $l = r\theta = 0.35 \times 2.4 = 0.84$ m.

questions.stem_md: An arc of length $5\pi$ cm on a circle of radius $12$ cm subtends an angle at the centre. Find this angle in degrees.
questions.solution_md: $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r} = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ radians, and $\dfrac{5\pi}{12} \times \dfrac{180}{\pi} = 75$ degrees.

questions.stem_md: The minute hand of a wall clock is $7$ cm long. How far, in centimetres, does its tip move in $20$ minutes? Take $\pi = 3.14159$ and give the answer to two decimal places.
questions.solution_md: In $20$ minutes the hand turns $\dfrac{20}{60}$ of a revolution, i.e. $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ radians. So $l = r\theta = 7 \times \dfrac{2 \times 3.14159}{3} = 14.66$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A toy trolley's wheel of radius $21$ cm rolls without slipping along a track in an imagined school laboratory and covers $1.47$ m. Find the angle through which the wheel turns, in radians, and the number of revolutions to two decimal places.

answer.model_answer_md:
Distance $= 1.47$ m $= 147$ cm. For rolling, $l = r\theta$, so $\theta = \dfrac{147}{21} = 7$ radians.

questions.stem_md: Two angles of a triangle are $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ radians. Find the third angle in radians and in degrees.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined observatories lie on the same meridian of the Earth, with latitudes differing by $9^\circ$. Taking the radius of the Earth as $6400$ km and $\pi = 3.14159$, find the distance between them along the meridian to the nearest kilometre.

questions.stem_md: Given $\tan\theta = -\dfrac{8}{15}$ and $\theta$ in the fourth quadrant, find the values of $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$, $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$, $\sec\theta$ and $\cot\theta$.

$\sin\theta = \tan\theta\cos\theta = -\dfrac{8}{15}\cdot\dfrac{15}{17} = -\dfrac{8}{17}$, so $\operatorname{cosec}\theta = -\dfrac{17}{8}$.

$\cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta} = -\dfrac{15}{8}$.

questions.stem_md: Prove that $\cos(x + y)\cos(x - y) = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 y$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Expand both factors: $(\cos x\cos y - \sin x\sin y)(\cos x\cos y + \sin x\sin y) = \cos^2 x\cos^2 y - \sin^2 x\sin^2 y$.

Replace $\cos^2 y = 1 - \sin^2 y$ and $\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x$:

$\cos^2 x(1 - \sin^2 y) - (1 - \cos^2 x)\sin^2 y = \cos^2 x - \cos^2 x\sin^2 y - \sin^2 y + \cos^2 x\sin^2 y = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 y$.

questions.stem_md: Use $75^\circ = 45^\circ + 30^\circ$ to show that $\tan 75^\circ = 2 + \sqrt{3}$.

questions.stem_md:
The point $P(\theta)$ of the unit circle is reached by turning through $\theta$ anticlockwise from the point $(1, 0)$.

(a) Write the exact coordinates of $P(120^\circ)$ and $P(315^\circ)$.

(b) Hence write $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$ and $\tan\theta$ for $\theta = 120^\circ$ and for $\theta = 315^\circ$.

(c) Verify that each point is at distance $1$ from the origin.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $P(\theta) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. For $120^\circ$ (quadrant II, reference angle $60^\circ$): $P = \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$. For $315^\circ$ (quadrant IV, reference angle $45^\circ$): $P = \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$.

**(b)** $\theta = 120^\circ$: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}/2}{-1/2} = -\sqrt{3}$.
$\theta = 315^\circ$: $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, $\tan\theta = -1$.

**(c)** $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} = 1$ and $\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)^2 + \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} = 1$, so both distances are $\sqrt{1} = 1$.

questions.solution_md: Coordinates of P are (cos, sin); then check x squared + y squared.

questions.stem_md:
The figure shows the graphs of $y = \sin x$ and $y = \cos x$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$. They meet at the points $P$ and $Q$.

(a) Show that at a meeting point $\tan x = 1$, and find the $x$-coordinates of $P$ and $Q$.

(b) Find the exact $y$-coordinates of $P$ and $Q$.

(c) For which values of $x$ in $[0, 2\pi]$ is $\sin x > \cos x$?

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** At a meeting point $\sin x = \cos x$. There $\cos x \ne 0$ (otherwise $\sin x$ would be $\pm 1$ as well), so dividing gives $\tan x = 1$. In $[0, 2\pi]$ the solutions are $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $x = \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{5\pi}{4}$.

**(b)** At $P$: $y = \sin\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$. At $Q$ (third quadrant): $y = \sin\dfrac{5\pi}{4} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

**(c)** Between the meeting points the sine curve lies above the cosine curve, as the figure shows (at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\sin x = 1 > 0 = \cos x$). So $\sin x > \cos x$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{4} < x < \dfrac{5\pi}{4}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Turning a quarter-turn more than $x$ swaps the roles of the coordinates: $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + x\right) = \cos x$. Turning half a turn more reverses both coordinates: $\cos(\pi + x) = -\cos x$. The angle $2\pi - x$ is the reflection of $x$ in the horizontal axis, so sine changes sign and cosine does not: $\tan(2\pi - x) = -\tan x$.

**(b)** $-1020^\circ + 3 \times 360^\circ = 60^\circ$, so $\sin(-1020^\circ) = \sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

$495^\circ - 360^\circ = 135^\circ$, in quadrant II where cosine is negative: $\cos 495^\circ = -\cos 45^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

$1305^\circ = 7 \times 180^\circ + 45^\circ$ and tangent has period $180^\circ$, so $\tan 1305^\circ = \tan 45^\circ = 1$.

Use $105^\circ = 60^\circ + 45^\circ$ for the following.

(a) Find the exact values of $\sin 105^\circ$ and $\cos 105^\circ$.

(b) Hence, or by the tangent formula, show that $\tan 105^\circ = -(2 + \sqrt{3})$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\sin 105^\circ = \sin 60^\circ\cos 45^\circ + \cos 60^\circ\sin 45^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{6}}{4}$.

$\cos 105^\circ = \cos 60^\circ\cos 45^\circ - \sin 60^\circ\sin 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{6}}{4}$.

**(b)** $\tan 105^\circ = \dfrac{\sin 105^\circ}{\cos 105^\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{6}} = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{1 - \sqrt{3}}$. Multiply by $\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{1 + \sqrt{3}}$: $\dfrac{(1 + \sqrt{3})^2}{1 - 3} = \dfrac{4 + 2\sqrt{3}}{-2} = -(2 + \sqrt{3})$.

**(c)** $\sin^2 105^\circ + \cos^2 105^\circ = \dfrac{(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{6})^2 + (\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{6})^2}{16} = \dfrac{(8 + 2\sqrt{12}) + (8 - 2\sqrt{12})}{16} = \dfrac{16}{16} = 1$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\cos 3x = \cos(2x + x) = \cos 2x\cos x - \sin 2x\sin x$. Use $\cos 2x = 2\cos^2 x - 1$ and $\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$:

$\cos 3x = (2\cos^2 x - 1)\cos x - 2\sin^2 x\cos x$. Put $\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x$:

$= 2\cos^3 x - \cos x - 2\cos x + 2\cos^3 x = 4\cos^3 x - 3\cos x$.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Prove that $\sin 3x = 4\sin x\,\sin(60^\circ - x)\,\sin(60^\circ + x)$.

(b) Hence find the exact value of $\sin 20^\circ\sin 40^\circ\sin 80^\circ$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\sin(60^\circ - x)\sin(60^\circ + x) = (\sin 60^\circ\cos x - \cos 60^\circ\sin x)(\sin 60^\circ\cos x + \cos 60^\circ\sin x) = \sin^2 60^\circ\cos^2 x - \cos^2 60^\circ\sin^2 x$.

With $\sin^2 60^\circ = \dfrac{3}{4}$ and $\cos^2 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{4}$: $\dfrac{3}{4}(1 - \sin^2 x) - \dfrac{1}{4}\sin^2 x = \dfrac{3}{4} - \sin^2 x$.

Therefore $4\sin x\sin(60^\circ - x)\sin(60^\circ + x) = 4\sin x\left(\dfrac{3}{4} - \sin^2 x\right) = 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x = \sin 3x$.

**(b)** Put $x = 20^\circ$: $\sin 60^\circ = 4\sin 20^\circ\sin 40^\circ\sin 80^\circ$, so $\sin 20^\circ\sin 40^\circ\sin 80^\circ = \dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{8}$.
